questions.question: How do you convert between strings and numbers in Go?
questions.title: Strconv Package
questions.direct_answer: strconv.Atoi("42") string→int (returns error); strconv.Itoa(7) int→string. NOT casting — parsing. ParseFloat, ParseBool, ParseInt(base) for the rest. The classic bug: string(42) is "*" (a RUNE), not "42".

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Strconv Package beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its complexity or failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Recall: strconv.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The string↔number boundary is strconv — parsing and formatting, always explicit:

```go
n, err := strconv.Atoi("42")             // string → int (error on bad input)
f, err := strconv.ParseFloat("3.14", 64)  // string → float64
s := strconv.Itoa(7)                       // int → string (can't fail)
```

Executed. Atoi on a bad string returns (0, error) — the comma-ok discipline.

Why Atoi and not a cast: Go conversions (float64(i), string(rune)) transform between representable forms; string→number is PARSING — the input can be invalid — so the API must answer 'did it work.' Hence (value, error).

The rest of the kit: ParseBool, ParseInt with base ("ff" in base 16), FormatFloat with verb ('f', 'e'), and the append-family (AppendInt onto []byte — allocation-free, what encoding/json uses internally).

The classic bug pair: Sprintf("%d") instead of Itoa (works, 3-5x slower); and string(n) instead of Itoa — string(65) is "A" (the RUNE 65), not "65" — the #1 beginner Go bug, which go vet flags.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    STR[string 42] --> |strconv.Atoi - PARSE| N[int 42]
    N --> |strconv.Itoa - FORMAT| STR
    N --> |string 42 - WRONG| CH[code point 42 = asterisk]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why this isn't a language cast — the categories: Go conversions (T(x)) transform between types whose REPRESENTATIONS are compatible (int→float64: widening; []byte↔string: encoding copy; named↔underlying: reinterpretation) — all compile-time-decidable. Parsing reads a TEXT FORM of unknown validity — "4x2" has no int value — so it's a function returning (value, error), not a conversion. Formatting writes a text form — can't fail for ints (Itoa).

The append-family and why it exists: strconv.AppendInt(buf, n, 10) formats onto an EXISTING []byte — no string allocation, reusable buffer. In hot paths (JSON encoders, loggers), the append-forms are why strconv shows up in every fast-formating library — encoding/json's own int encoder is AppendInt. The allocation chain of Itoa (format into temp → allocate string → copy) becomes one buffer write.

The string(n) trap, fully: string takes a rune (int32 code point) and yields its character — string(65) is "A", NOT "65". The beginner writes string(userCount) and gets a rune-jumble (42 becomes '*' — code point 42). go vet has a dedicated check for this, and the classic writeups call it one of Go's most common first-week bugs — silent wrong text, no error. The discipline: number→string is ALWAYS Itoa/Sprintf, never string().

questions.question: What does ParseInt's bitSize argument do?
questions.title: When would you use Strconv Package in a real project
questions.direct_answer: The bit width of the result (0, 8, 16, 32, 64): ParseInt("ff", 16, 8) fails (255 > int8 max); bitSize 64 succeeds. It bounds the range — a range check before returning.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: The bit width of the result (0, 8, 16, 32, 64): ParseInt("ff", 16, 8) fails (255 > int8 max); bitSize 64 succeeds. It bounds the range — a range check.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
ParseInt takes (string, base, bitSize). The bitSize bounds what value can come back:

```go
n, err := strconv.ParseInt("255", 10, 8)   // fails: 255 > int8 max (127)
m, err := strconv.ParseInt("255", 10, 16)  // 255 — fits int16
hex, err := strconv.ParseInt("ff", 16, 32)   // 255 — parsed in base 16
```

Executed. The bitSize is a RANGE VALIDATOR — the parse succeeds on well-formed input, then the value is checked against the type's bounds (0 = int/platform, 8 = int8, 16 = int16, 32 = int32, 64 = int64).

Where it matters in real code: validating user input against a column type or protocol field — 'this ID must fit a uint32' becomes ParseInt(s, 10, 32) with the error doing the rejection. It's the parse-and-validate in one call.

The relationship to Atoi: Atoi(s) is exactly ParseInt(s, 10, 0) — decimal, platform int. The shorthand exists because it's 90% of the use; ParseInt is the full control (base + bounds).

The unsigned counterpart: ParseUint with the same shape — and the negative-number asymmetry (ParseUint("-1") fails by definition).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P[ParseInt s base bitSize] --> D[decode digits]
    D --> CHK{value in range?}
    CHK --> |yes| R[return value]
    CHK --> |no| ER[error: out of range]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The mechanics: the parser produces an arbitrary-precision intermediate, then checks it against the bitSize's range (math.MinInt8..MaxInt8 for 8, etc.) before returning — the check is POST-parse, so the error distinguishes 'malformed number' (syntax) from 'valid number, wrong range' (range) by the same error pathway — the error message differs (invalid syntax vs value out of range), which is the detail that lets callers give the right user-facing message.

Why bitSize 0 means 'int': the platform's int (64 on modern systems, 32 on some embedded) — 0 defers to the native width. Code that must be portable across 32-bit targets uses explicit 64 for wide values (parsing a timestamp on a 32-bit platform with bitSize 0 fails for values past 2^31 — the portability bug).

The base parameter's full semantics: 0 means 'infer from prefix' (0x → hex, 0 → octal, else decimal) — matching Go source literals; 1 is invalid; 2-36 explicit. The infer-mode is how ParseInt handles the same strings Go itself parses — the CL flag and config world where "0x1F" and "0755" appear as written. Choosing base 10 explicitly when the input ISN'T Go-source-shaped avoids the surprise of "010" parsing as 8 (octal) rather than 10 — the classic input-validation footgun.

questions.question: How do you parse a bool from a string in Go?
questions.title: a common mistake when using Strconv Package
questions.direct_answer: strconv.ParseBool: accepts "1", "t", "T", "true", "TRUE", "True" (and the falsy set) — case variations of the truthy words. NOT just "true"/"false" — the wider set comes from strconv's own conventions.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: strconv.ParseBool: accepts "1", "t", "T", "true", "TRUE", "True" (and the falsy set) — case variations of the truthy words. NOT just "true"/"false" — the wider set comes from strconv's own.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
ParseBool accepts the short forms:

```go
b, err := strconv.ParseBool("true")   // true, nil
b, err := strconv.ParseBool("1")      // true, nil
b, err := strconv.ParseBool("T")      // true, nil
b, err := strconv.ParseBool("yes")    // false, error — not in the set
```

The truthy set: "1", "t", "T", "true", "TRUE", "True". The falsy set: "0", "f", "F", "false", "FALSE", "False". Anything else is an error.

Why this particular set: it matches strconv's own FormatBool round-trip and the common single-letter conventions (t/f) from config-file formats and CLIs. The set is fixed — you can't extend it.

For OTHER truthy vocabularies ("yes"/"no", "on"/"off", "y"/"n"), ParseBool doesn't help — that's a map lookup or a switch you write:

```go
var truths = map[string]bool{"yes": true, "on": true, "y": true}
```

The design note: Go puts the strict, mechanical parse in the stdlib and leaves the human-vocabulary handling to the app — consistent with strconv's everywhere-explicit philosophy.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    T[1 t T true TRUE True] --> B[true]
    F[0 f F false FALSE False] --> B2[false]
    X[anything else] --> ER[error - your app maps]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The round-trip contract as the design driver: FormatBool(b) produces 'true'/'false' (lowercase only), and ParseBool accepts those — plus the wider short forms. The asymmetry (format is narrow, parse is wide) is the deliberate pattern: produce canonical output, accept liberal input — Postel's law applied at the function level. The same pattern appears in ParseInt (accepts prefixes) and time parsing (RFC3339 strict, but the layout system is liberal in what layouts exist).

The error shape: ParseBool's error is a *NumError carrying (Func: "ParseBool", Num: input, Err: ErrSyntax) — the strconv error type across the family. The structured error lets callers distinguish 'bad syntax' from 'out of range' (ParseInt family) — for ParseBool, syntax is the only failure. errors.Is(err, strconv.ErrSyntax) is the idiomatic branch — the sentinel pattern the errors topic covered, appearing inside strconv's small API.

Where ParseBool appears in the wild: encoding/json's own boolean parsing converges to the same true/false set; CL flag parsing (flag package) uses its own narrower set; config libraries (viper, yaml) implement the wider yes/no/on/off maps on top. Knowing ParseBool's fixed vocabulary answers 'why does my yes/no config fail to parse' — the stdlib's answer is strict; the human vocabulary is your layer.

questions.question: What is the difference between strconv.ParseFloat's bitSize 32 and 64?
questions.title: compare Strconv Package with an alternative
questions.direct_answer: The precision of the result: 64 gives float64 (full precision), 32 gives float32 (rounded, smaller range). Use 64 unless a protocol/column demands 32. The VALUE differs: ParseFloat("3.14", 32) != float64(ParseFloat("3.14", 64)).

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: The precision of the result: 64 gives float64 (full precision), 32 gives float32 (rounded, smaller range). Use 64 unless a protocol/column demands 32. The VALUE differs: ParseFloat("3.14", 32) != float64(ParseFloat("3.14".

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
bitSize selects the target precision:

```go
f64, _ := strconv.ParseFloat("3.14", 64)  // float64 — full precision
f32, _ := strconv.ParseFloat("3.14", 32)  // float32 — rounded to 24-bit mantissa
```

Executed in the earlier verification: f64 = 3.14 (the nearest float64). f32 = 3.140000104904175 — wait, actually the float32 nearest 3.14, which printed as float64 shows the rounding gap. The point: they hold DIFFERENT values from the same input.

When 32 is right: the value is destined for a float32 storage (a protocol field, a column typed REAL, a graphics/API that consumes float32) — parse directly to the target precision so the rounding happens once, at the boundary. When 64 is right: everything else — Go's default float is float64, and math functions, literals, and constants assume it.

The float32 subtlety that bites: float64(f32) doesn't recover the input — the precision was lost at the parse. A pipeline that parses to 32, computes in 64, and outputs '3.14' gets 3.140000104904175 — the stored error propagates. Parse to the precision you'll keep, or parse to 64 and narrow deliberately at the edge.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    F2[%.2f - fixed decimals]
    G[%g - shortest round-trip]
    B[binary 0.1] --> |actual value| T[0.10000000000000000555...]
    T --> |%g| P[0.1 - shortest that round-trips]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The precision mechanics: float32 has a 24-bit significand (~7 decimal digits); float64 has 53 (~15-17 digits). ParseFloat's algorithm (a correct-rounding decimal-to-binary conversion — the same family of algorithms as formatting's shortest-round-trip, run in reverse) produces the NEAREST representable value of the chosen width. The 'nearest' differs by width: 3.14's nearest float32 and nearest float64 are different real numbers, both approximating 3.14 — hence the different values from the same string.

The interface boundary story: JSON's number type parses as float64 in encoding/json (the width was chosen once, for the whole ecosystem); databases vary (REAL/float4 columns want 32 — the driver handles the narrowing); GPU/ML protocols often specify 32. The parse's bitSize should match the STORAGE, because storage is where the rounding becomes permanent — the 'round once, at the edge' principle (the same discipline as the money-int pattern: convert precisely, store exactly, format late).

The comparison trap worth one line in any answer: two floats parsed from the same string at different widths are equal only if the string happened to be exactly representable in both ('0.5' — a power of two — is; '3.14' isn't). The equality-past-the-boundary question (the floats topic) is downstream of this parse-time choice — yet another place where the earlier decision (bitSize) becomes the later bug.

questions.question: How do you format a number with commas (thousands separators) in Go?
questions.title: debug a problem involving Strconv Package
questions.direct_answer: No stdlib function does it directly. golang.org/x/text/message prints with locale separators (message.NewPrinter(language.English).Sprintf("%d", n)). The manual pattern: chunk digits in groups of 3 from the right.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Recall: No stdlib function does it directly.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The standard library fmt/strconv don't include grouping — it's a locale concern, and Go keeps locale out of the core. The options, in order of correctness:

The x/text route (the official answer):

```go
import "golang.org/x/text/message"
import "golang.org/x/text/language"

p := message.NewPrinter(language.English)
p.Sprintf("%d", 1234567)   // "1,234,567"
```

Locale-aware by construction (English commas, German periods, Hindi's grouping rules) — the right answer when the output is user-facing.

The manual route (no dependency, fixed format):

```go
func comma(s string) string {
    // sign, chunk from the right in 3s, join with ","
}
```

The manual version is exact and small — but it hard-codes ONE convention. If the audience is always English-format, that's fine; if not, x/text.

What NOT to do: Sprintf has no grouping verb (%d never inserts commas — there's no flag for it) and strconv doesn't either. Regex-based insertion (matching digit triples from the right) works but is the slow, clever version of what the manual loop does directly.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    N[1234567] --> |x/text message| F[1,234,567]
    N --> |plain %d| F2[1234567 - no grouping in fmt]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why the core library omits grouping — the i18n rationale: thousands separators are LOCALE data (English: 1,234,567.89; German: 1.234.567,89; some locales group the first 3 then 2 — Hindi 12,34,567). fmt deliberately has no locale model — its output is machine-stable across systems. The entire locale surface lives in x/text (message, language, number) — the standard library's separation of 'mechanical formatting' from 'human-cultural formatting.' That's why the answer to 'how do I add commas' is really 'which package owns locale concerns' — x/text.

message.Printer's mechanics: it wraps fmt with a locale context — the same verbs, but %d and %f consult the locale's number rules. Underneath, x/text/number implements the CLDR grouping algorithms (the Unicode consortium's locale data — the same data ICU and every i18n library uses). The Printer composes: formatting verbs (fmt) + locale rules (CLDR data) + caching (the printer reuses parsed locale state).

The pragmatic tiers, restated for an interview answer: (1) machine-readable / log output — plain %d, no grouping, always; (2) fixed-format human display (an internal tool, an English-only report) — the manual comma loop, ~10 lines, zero dependencies; (3) real locale-aware UI — x/text/message, the CLDR-backed answer. Choosing tier 1 when you meant tier 3 is the bug (logs that were supposed to be reports); choosing tier 3 for tier 1 needs is the over-engineering (pulling the i18n stack into a CLI).
